blocks.prompt: How the Ground Folds Up
blocks.text: A mountain is not just a big pile of rocks. It is the ground pushed up from below. The Earth's skin is broken into huge plates. The plates move very slowly. When two plates push into each other, the ground between them has nowhere to go. So it crumples up. It folds like a rug when you push it across the floor. That fold is a mountain. It takes millions of years. The mountain is still being pushed up today. Wind and rain wear the top down at the same time. The mountain grows and wears away, over and over, for a very long time.

blocks.prompt: Seashells on the Roof of the World
blocks.text: Mount Everest is the highest place on Earth. Its top stands 29,032 feet above the sea. If you climbed all the way up and looked at the rock under your boots, you would find something strange. Seashells. The stone at the very top of Everest is full of the shells of sea creatures that died on an ocean floor. They are not a trick. That rock really was an ocean floor once. Around 50 million years ago, the land we now call India was an island drifting north across the sea. It crashed slowly into Asia. The ocean between them was squeezed shut. Its floor had nowhere to go but up. The crash is still happening. India is still pushing north, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Everest rises a few millimeters higher every year. So the highest rock in the world used to be the lowest, and the shells of small sea animals now sit in the coldest wind on the planet.

4.title: The Mountain That Is Still Growing

4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Mountain That Is Still Growing

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Air cools about 3.5 degrees per 1,000 feet

blocks.prompt: The Sky Gets Colder as You Climb
blocks.text: Climbing a mountain is a strange kind of travel. You walk a few miles and the world changes as much as it would if you drove a thousand miles north. Start at the bottom, in warm forest. Keep going. The trees get shorter and tougher. Then they stop altogether, at a line you can see from far away, called the tree line. Above it there is only rock, moss, and snow that never melts. The reason is the air. Most people think high places are closer to the sun and should be warmer, but the sun is 93 million miles away, so a few miles up makes no difference at all. What matters is that air holds heat poorly and the ground holds it well. Sunlight warms the dirt and rock, and the ground warms the air above it. High on a mountain there is less ground and less air to hold that heat. There is a second reason. Air is squeezed by the weight of the air above it. Climb higher and there is less weight, so the air spreads out, and air that spreads out cools down. Every thousand feet you climb, the air drops about three and a half degrees. This is why the same mountain can be green on one side and bare on the other. Wind pushes wet air up the slope. The air cools, the water falls out as rain or snow, and dry air slides down the far side. Behind many mountain ranges lies a desert.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Most of a mountain sits underground
Crust under the Himalayas runs over 40 miles deep

blocks.prompt: Why Mountains Cannot Grow Forever
blocks.text: A mountain range looks like the most permanent thing on Earth. It is actually a temporary bulge, and it is losing. Mountains rise where the crust is squeezed. When two of the plates that make up Earth's outer shell collide, neither one can move aside, so the rock between them thickens and buckles upward. The Himalayas are the wreckage of India driving into Asia. The Andes rise where the floor of the Pacific slides beneath South America. The Alps mark Africa pressing north into Europe. In each case, the mountains are simply crust with nowhere else to go. But there is a limit, and it is not strength. It is buoyancy. Earth's crust floats on the hot, slow-flowing rock of the mantle beneath it, the way an iceberg floats in the sea. Most of an iceberg is underwater. In the same way, most of a mountain is underground. Beneath the Himalayas the crust reaches down more than forty miles, a root far larger than the peaks above it. Pile on more rock and the root sinks deeper. The mountain cannot simply keep climbing. Meanwhile the sky is taking it apart. Water seeps into cracks, freezes, and splits the rock. Rivers carry the pieces away. Glaciers grind whole valleys into new shapes. The higher a range rises, the harder the weather hits it, and the faster it comes down. Uplift and erosion argue with each other, and for a while they roughly balance. Then the pushing stops. When the plates finally settle, only erosion is left, and erosion never stops. The range wears lower and lower. As the load is removed, the deep root floats slowly upward, lifting fresh rock into the weather to be worn away in turn. You can see the ending in the eastern United States. The Appalachian Mountains are old, soft, green, and rounded, and nobody would mistake them for the Himalayas. Roughly 300 million years ago, though, they were built by the same kind of collision, and they may well have stood as high. Everything above the modern summits has been carried, grain by grain, into the sea.

6.title: The Mountain That Is Still Growing
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Mountain That Is Still Growing

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Air is 21 percent oxygen at any altitude
Everest's summit pressure is about a third of sea level
The death zone begins near 26,000 feet
Chimborazo's peak is farthest from Earth's center
Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas
Tibetans carry a high-altitude gene from Denisovans

blocks.prompt: The Thin Air Problem
blocks.text: Ask which mountain is highest and the answer sounds simple. Mount Everest, 29,032 feet. But height has to be measured from somewhere, and sea level is only one choice. The Earth is not a sphere. It spins, and the spin makes it bulge at the equator, so the ground there starts out farther from the planet's core. Chimborazo, a peak in Ecuador, rises only about 20,500 feet above the sea, yet its summit sits more than a mile farther from the center of the Earth than Everest's does. Both facts are true. They are just answers to different questions. Everest still wins the question that matters to a human body, because the body does not care about the center of the Earth. It cares about pressure. Here is the part almost everyone gets wrong. The air on top of Everest is not short of oxygen. It is 21 percent oxygen, exactly like the air in your room, exactly like the air over the sea. What changes is how tightly it is packed. Air has weight, and the air at sea level is being squashed by the entire column of atmosphere stacked above it. Climb, and you leave most of that column below you. At the summit of Everest the pressure is about a third of what it is at the beach. Take a full breath there and you get a third of the molecules. The percentage never moved. The pressure did. A body fights back. Within days at altitude, breathing quickens and the kidneys release a hormone that tells the bone marrow to build more red blood cells. Given weeks, most people can adapt enough to function surprisingly high. But above roughly 26,000 feet, adaptation fails. Climbers call it the death zone, and the name is not drama. Up there the body cannot repair itself faster than the thin air breaks it down. You are not resting. You are running down a clock. Which makes the exceptions worth staring at. Bar-headed geese migrate straight across the Himalayas, beating their wings in air that would knock a person unconscious. Their hemoglobin grabs oxygen more tightly than ours, their lungs move air more efficiently, and their flight muscles are packed with the machinery to burn it. People have their own versions, and they are not the same as each other. Highlanders in the Andes carry thick blood loaded with extra red cells, the brute-force solution, and it costs them: blood that thick is slow and dangerous. Tibetans went another way entirely. They do not overload their blood. They breathe faster and keep their vessels wide, moving ordinary blood more quickly. The gene behind much of this is called EPAS1, and when researchers traced the Tibetan version of it, they found it did not come from ordinary human ancestors at all. It came from Denisovans, a vanished human cousin, and it entered our species tens of thousands of years ago. So the mountain does something no gym can. It sets a problem the body cannot bluff its way past, and it keeps the answers on file. Everest is not just the highest rock. It is the clearest place on Earth to watch what living things will do when the air runs out.
